title: Voters pass 37 of 41 local measures restricting AI data centers
subtitle: The November 3 midterms produced the largest single-day vote against data-center expansion on record, with Ohio accounting for more than half of the ballot items.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: On November 3, voters in ten US states decided 41 local ballot measures on AI data-center development. Thirty-seven limited or blocked projects, one supported development — in Harwood, North Dakota, where residents rejected a proposal requiring extra review of industrial projects by about three to one — and the remainder are still being counted. Ohio accounted for 21 of the 41 measures across 18 municipalities. In Wilmington, Ohio, roughly 80% of voters rejected rezonings tied to a planned data-center project across four separate referendums. In Edgewater, Florida, voters approved a charter amendment prohibiting data centers outright. In Wells, Maine, more than 80% of voters approved a retroactive 180-day moratorium.

The vote is the first time the data-center boom has been measured at the ballot box at this scale. Prior opposition had been visible but localized — a county planning commission here, a utility rate case there. Putting the question directly to voters in dozens of jurisdictions on the same day produced a near-uniform answer: residents will approve bans, moratoria, and rezonings aimed at slowing or stopping hyperscale projects, even in places that have historically welcomed large industrial employers. The results do not stop existing projects already permitted, but they tighten the siting problem for everything in the pipeline.

The backlash has three threads pulling together — electricity prices, water use, and local control. Utility commissions in several Midwestern states have approved rate structures that pass the cost of data-center-driven grid upgrades to residential ratepayers. Groundwater withdrawals for cooling have become a visible issue in drier regions. And residents have learned to read zoning agendas that two years ago felt invisible. The combination gives any local campaigner a viable template, which is why 40 of 41 measures lining up the same way is less a surprise than a signal. Expect the pattern to repeat in December, when additional votes are scheduled in Arkansas and North Dakota.

A note for learners: the economics of frontier AI depend on gigawatts of new electrical capacity in the next five years. The headline forecasts — Goldman's latest $8.5 trillion data-center build-out estimate among them — assume a permitting environment that these votes are pulling in the other direction. If you are modeling AI infrastructure, compute economics, or the climate implications of the buildout, the local political layer is no longer a rounding error. Any model that assumes smooth siting in the base case is already wrong. The interesting question is where the industry puts the next 50 GW given which jurisdictions are now closed.
